short_answer: Jim Feist is a real and very old name in the pick selling business. His own site names him, gives a Las Vegas mailing address and phone number, and sells a 30 day all sports package. The same picks are also sold through Capper Reviews, a site that says it is part of the SportsCapping network, with a full price list. In that narrow sense the service is legitimate.

Whether the picks make money is a separate question, and nothing we could open answers it. The sales pages show streaks such as "MLB Money Lines (+6710) 1016-879" and "62-46 run with my last 111 Football picks," chosen by the seller, and a table of the previous day's plays. We found no full, time stamped log of every pick that we could check.

Treat Jim Feist as a famous seller with marketing records, not a proven winner. Prices for similar packages differ a lot between the two storefronts, so compare before you pay, and record every pick yourself with the line and time you got it.
pricing_intro: The first row was on jimfeist.com on 7 Nov 2026. Capper Reviews, a reseller that says it is part of the SportsCapping network, lists more Jim Feist packages and single plays, but a reseller listing is not a verified current offer from Jim Feist, so we do not quote those prices.

Free extra time only, and no guarantee on season passes, per the network policy
guarantee: On the Capper Reviews page, short and multi day packages say they are "guaranteed to show a profit" or the buyer gets the same period again free. The network guarantee policy explains the limits: no extra time if the package made any profit at all, grading on 100 unit intervals, only one free period per purchase even if the free period also loses, and "There is NO GUARANTEE on seasonal subscriptions." It also says plainly that it does not offer a money back policy.

On jimfeist.com, the $149 30 day package page states no guarantee, and the site terms mention a refund only when the store itself cancels an order. A buyer who loses money betting the picks gets, at best, more picks. Losses on the bets themselves are never covered, and they are usually far larger than the package price.

claims_note: The experience claim changes with the page. The About page says over five decades, the jimfeist.com product page says "over 55 years," the Capper Reviews package blurbs call him a 60 year veteran, and the Capper Reviews bio still says "more than 30 years." None of these proves anything about the picks, but the copy is not kept consistent.

The bio cites contest wins without naming one. The only contest detail we found was a 2022 Gambling911 article in which another handicapper said he made the picks for a 1985 Castaways football contest entry that Jim Feist paid for, and split the prize with him. That is one man's account, not a record.

Each streak on the Capper Reviews page starts on a date the seller chose, from 2014 to 2026 judging by the page links, and the dollar figures assume a stake the page does not explain. A streak cut from a longer history tells you little; every handicapper has a hot stretch somewhere.
record: What a buyer can verify independently: nothing that we could find. We found no full, time stamped log of every Jim Feist pick with the line, the odds and the release time, no third party contest results we could open, and no court or regulator record about the service.

What the seller publishes: the Capper Reviews page shows streak totals by sport and a "Yesterday's plays" table with results and write ups. On 7 Nov 2026 it listed a lost over 50 in Nebraska at Illinois and a won under 39.5 in South Florida at East Carolina. These are graded by the same network that sells the picks, on the odds the handicapper selected, so they are the seller's own marketing, not an audit.
jimfeist.com shows no record at all on the pages we read. Its free picks page asked us to sign in.

our_data.text: Watchdog grades picks captured from public posts before the game starts. In this edition no Jim Feist pick history is matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how Jim Feist performs.
our_data.context: For scale: the streaks on the Capper Reviews page run from 54% to 74% winners. On the Watchdog board on 7 Nov 2026, {{over60}} of {{established}} established accounts (100 or more graded picks) were at 60% or better, and the median established account won {{median_win}}% of its picks. At standard -110 odds a bettor needs about 52.4% to break even.

customers_intro: Independent customer evidence on Jim Feist is thin and mostly old. The biggest pool of comments sits on a site that is part of the network selling his picks. Below is everything we found and how much weight it can carry.

customers.text: The Capper Reviews page shows a rating of 3.91 out of 5 from 55 votes and 22 undated comments. Most comments praise his longevity and free picks, a few complain that he is too old or plays too many games in a day. Capper Reviews says it is part of the network that sells these packages, so this is not independent evidence.
On HandicappingReviews.org, a reviewer named William wrote that the service took his $500 and called it a scam. He gave no details or results, and we could not verify the complaint.

On the same page, a reviewer named Nicholas said he bought the picks for about 10 weeks and called the company legitimate. He did not say whether he won. The site's own undated review says his reputation has not delivered great results recently.

In an SBR forum thread where a bettor asked about paid pick services, one member mentioned in passing that Jim Feist was "back," while the replies around it told the poster not to pay any tout. Nobody posted results for Feist.

A Better Business Bureau search for Jim Feist in Las Vegas returned no results, SmartCustomer lists jimfeist.com with zero reviews, and Trustpilot blocked our check. Our searches found no Reddit or TheRX thread about the service, and two older SBR threads about Feist did not open for us.

conflicts: Capper Reviews, the page with the full price list and the star rating, says it is part of the SportsCapping network that processes the sale. Its rating and comments therefore come from the seller's side of the deal.

The same Capper Reviews page carried a banner for a "$1,000 Free Play at MyBookie" that links through an affiliate tracking address. Affiliate deals usually pay the referrer when referred customers sign up or lose. That does not prove anything about the picks, but it is a financial interest a buyer should know about.
MyBookie is an offshore sportsbook, and offshore sportsbooks are not licensed by U.S. state regulators. Check the law where you live. We saw no sportsbook links on the jimfeist.com pages we read.
strengths: A named seller with a Las Vegas mailing address, a phone number and written site terms.
Prices are published for every package on both storefronts, and the network guarantee rules are written out in detail.
His own store shows one clear price: $149 for 30 days of all sports.
concerns: No full public record. Every number we saw is a streak or total chosen by the seller.
The guarantee gives more picks, never money back, and season passes have no guarantee at all.
The jimfeist.com product title and price disagree ($199 versus $149), and the reseller lists its own, different package range.
Experience claims change from page to page, and contest wins are claimed without being named.
The reseller page that hosts the rating also carries an offshore sportsbook affiliate banner.
checklist: Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Count units, not wins. A 60% record at heavy favorites can still lose money.
Read the guarantee for the words refund, credit and extension. Most "guarantees" in this business are credits.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get.
Give any handicapper a few hundred picks before you call them a winner. Short runs swing hard both ways.
faq: He is a real, long running seller with a named Las Vegas address, published prices and his own store. We could not verify that his picks win over time, because he does not publish a full record of every pick, and we found no court or regulator action involving him.
How much does Jim Feist cost?
On 7 Nov 2026 jimfeist.com sold 30 days of all sports for $149. A reseller network lists other Jim Feist packages, but a reseller listing is not a verified current offer from Jim Feist.
Does Jim Feist have a verified record?
No. The sales pages show streaks such as 1016-879 on MLB money lines and a table of yesterday's plays, all published by the selling network. We found no independent, time stamped log of every pick.

For the money you get every play he releases in the period you buy, from one of the oldest names in the business, and on short packages a free repeat period if you lose. What is unproven is whether his picks beat the roughly 52.4% needed at -110 over hundreds of plays, and nothing refunds the package or your betting losses.
